2025 — present UFF Media Lab

Vivenciando o Passado

Educational VR built with a UNESCO Chair, on the Atlantic slave trade

  • RoleProject Lead · Game Designer · Developer
  • TeamFour programmers, reporting to me, alongside a 3D artist and a team of historians
  • TimelineMay 2025 — present
  • StatusIn development
  • Built withUnity · C# · Unity XR · Google Sheets integration · Mixamo
UFF Media Lab

The project

An immersive VR and mixed-reality experience that places a school student inside the logistics of the Atlantic slave trade in 1830s Rio de Janeiro. Five scenes — a slave ship, the Customs docks, the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, the Valongo Wharf, and a slave shop on the Rua do Valongo — are reconstructed from historical and archaeological sources and experienced first-person, from the point of view of a child. It is built at UFF Media Lab with the Instituto de História and the UNESCO Chair on Global and Social Inequalities, aligned to the Brazilian national curriculum, and designed to work for learners with ADHD. It is exhibited in mixed reality at Casa da Descoberta in Niterói.

What I owned

  • Lead the four-person programming team — task breakdown, prioritisation, running the meetings, and holding the milestones.
  • Built the dialogue system and wired it to a Google Sheet, so the project's historians could write and revise every character line themselves without a programmer in the loop.
  • Built out scenes, and imported and configured the character animation from Mixamo.
  • Ran the client relationship: turned what the historians wanted into technical design decisions, and coordinated with the 3D artist.
  • Delegated the remaining scene work, optimisation and shader tasks.

A problem I solved

The concept did not survive contact with VR. As specified, the scenes were tight interiors with almost no player movement and very dark environments — three things that make a VR experience uncomfortable, disorienting and inert. I could not simply implement the brief. I also could not overrule it, because the historical accuracy *was* the project; this is teaching material about slavery, not a game with a historical skin.

So I worked through it with the historians scene by scene, separating the constraints that were load-bearing historically from the ones that were incidental. Where the sources allowed it we opened up sightlines and circulation. We gave the player things to do with their hands instead of only things to look at. And we raised light levels to the point where a scene stayed readable without becoming wrong.

Result

Five scenes a classroom can actually be walked through, without giving up the documentary basis the project exists to deliver. The dialogue system turned out to matter as much as anything visual: it removed the programmer bottleneck from a project whose content experts are historians, so the script could keep being revised right up to the exhibition.
